# Mahāsamaya Sutta (DN 20 (PTS DN ii 253))

**ID:** DN 20 (PTS DN ii 253)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsamaya Sutta
**PTS:** DN ii 253
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul6.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsamaya Sutta* ("The Great Congregation", DN 20) is the twentieth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya*, set in the Great Wood (*Mahāvana*) at Kapilavatthu in the Sakyan territory [Skilling 1993]. The word *samaya* in the title denotes a meeting or "concourse", explained by the commentary as a "great assembly" (*mahāsamūha*) [Bodhi 2000]. The narrative background recounts how the Buddha mediated a conflict between the Sakyans and Koliyans over the waters of the Rohiṇī River, after which five hundred youths went forth and attained arahantship, assembling before the Buddha on the full-moon night of Jeṭṭhamūla [Bodhi 2000]. When deities from across the realms gathered to pay homage, the Buddha uttered verses naming and describing the assembled gods, yakkhas, and spirits [Williams 2000]. Providing one of the most extensive catalogues of deities in early Indian Buddhism, these verses became a central protective text (*paritta* / *rakṣā*), commonly chanted throughout Theravādin traditions and included among the recitations of the *Catubhāṇavāra* [Holz 2022].

Curated parallels and DharmaNexus matches show wide cross-canonical transmission [DharmaNexus]. Direct Sanskrit parallels, titled *Mahāsamājasūtra*, are preserved among Central Asian manuscript fragments edited by Ernst Waldschmidt [Nakamura 1980; Skilling 1992]. Two distinct Tibetan translations exist in the Kanjur: an early translation of the Mūlasarvāstivādin *Mahāsamājasūtra* (D 34) executed around 800 CE by Jinamitra, Prajñāvarman, and Ye shes sde, and a 14th-century translation by Ānandaśrī and Nyi ma rgyal mtshan that translates directly from a Theravādin text and preserves the title *Mahāsamaya-sūtra* [Skilling 1992; Skilling 1993]. Chinese translations include *Dà sānmó rě jīng* (大三摩惹經, T 19) and DĀ 19, alongside Samyuktāgama versions (SĀ 1192; SĀ² 105) [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, the opening prose and verse portions are identical with SN 1.37 in the *Devatā Saṁyutta*, and passages are closely shared with the *Āṭānāṭiya Sutta* (DN 32) and the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16) [Bodhi 2000; DharmaNexus].
